results.title: Render alternative for agent sandboxes: CreateOS
results.content:
Files survive: a sandbox keeps its filesystem until you destroy it, while Render discards local filesystem changes on redeploy.
 Pause and fork a live environment, which Render does not publish for running instances.
 Outbound allowlists by host, IP or CIDR, enforced outside the VM. Render does not publish an egress default.
 No egress fees, against Render's $0.15/GB once included bandwidth runs out (each sandbox has a 50 GiB budget by default).

Where Renderis strong

A complete managed stack in one place: web services, background workers, cron jobs, managed Postgres with point-in-time recovery and preview environments, with compute prorated to the second.

## Which to pick

Pick CreateOS Sandbox if [...] ## Which to pick

Pick CreateOS Sandbox if

 Your agent needs a disposable machine per task, not a deployed service
 You want to pause a session and resume it later with memory intact
 You want to restrict outbound traffic to a list of hosts

Pick Render if

 You run a production web app with a database and want no servers to manage
 You need preview environments per pull request
 You need service machines up to 12 CPU / 96 GB

## Head-to-head comparison

Every dimension side by side, checked on 17 October 2026 against each vendor's own docs and pricing pages. "Not published" means we could not find it on the vendor's pages, not that the feature is missing. [...] | Dimension | CreateOS Sandbox | Render |
 --- 
| Built for | API-created sandboxes for agent-written and untrusted code | Production web services, workers, cron jobs, Postgres and Key Value |
| Isolation | Firecracker micro-VM with its own guest kernel | Not published |
| Ephemeral per-run environments | Yes. Create a sandbox per task by API, SDK, CLI or MCP and destroy it after | Not the model; services are deployed and long-running. Preview environments per pull request |
| Pause and resume | Yes. Saves disk, memory and CPU state; vCPU stops billing while paused, memory and storage still bill | Not published; Free services spin down after 15 minutes idle and take about one minute to spin back up (vendor-stated) |

results.content:
The practical cost difference comes from standby behavior. Sandboxes don't accrue compute charges while idle. For the normalized baseline, exact active-hour pricing depends on the current sandbox tier, while standby carries zero compute cost.

### Who is Blaxel best for?

Blaxel fits coding agents first. Webflow uses it for AI coding workflows and real-time previews. It also handles PR review agents like Delty and code modification agents like Jazzberry.

## 2. Modal

Modal is a Python-native serverless platform. Its Sandboxes product runs isolated containers for AI code and reinforcement learning rollouts. It offers sandbox concurrency above 100,000 concurrent sandboxes with sub-second scheduling. [...] Its sandboxes run as microVMs built on Blaxel's custom fork of Firecracker. Sandboxes transition to standby after approximately 15 seconds of inactivity. They stay there indefinitely at zero compute cost. Blaxel is a first-class sandbox provider in the OpenAI Agents SDK. The SDK builds on OpenAI's Codex harness, while Blaxel Sandboxes handle the execution layer.

Blaxel's feature set centers on state, isolation, and agent-operated lifecycle control: [...] TL;DR:

results.title: DeployHQ Managed VPS vs Render: Real Linux vs PaaS Sandbox
results.content:
## TL;DR

If your application fits a PaaS shape — stateless web service, managed Postgres, autoscaling on CPU thresholds, no need to SSH into the box — Render is the cleaner answer. The PaaS model removes a meaningful amount of operational work, and Render's product surface is mature and well-designed.

If you need a real Linux box — for SSH access, custom services, cron jobs, third-party agents (monitoring, log shipping, backups), or any workload that needs to step outside a sandbox — DeployHQ Managed VPS is the right product. You get a real Ubuntu VPS plus the DeployHQ deployment pipeline already wrapped around it.

For broader context, our roundup of the best software deployment tools in 2026 places Render, DeployHQ, and the rest of the category side by side. [...] The right choice depends on whether your workload needs real Linux (custom services, SSH access, anything outside a PaaS sandbox) or whether the PaaS abstraction's constraints are actually freedoms — fewer decisions to make, less operational surface to maintain.

This guide is a head-to-head comparison: features, pricing, lock-in, and when each one wins. (For broader Heroku-replacement framing — Render alongside Railway and Fly.io — our Heroku alternatives in 2026 roundup covers the wider migration story.)

## TL;DR [...] Render is excellent for canonical PaaS workloads — stateless web services, standard runtimes, managed databases. It removes operational work in exchange for runtime constraints. Most CRUD apps fit this shape comfortably.
 DeployHQ Managed VPS is excellent when the PaaS shape doesn't fit — when you need root access, custom services, third-party agents, or any workload that needs to step outside a sandbox. It's a real Linux box with deployment automation wrapped around it.
